It is recommended to avoid co-administration or use an alternative medication due to the risk of thromboembolic disorders. 2. Repotrectinib decreases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by inducing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 enzymes. This can significantly reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Female patients should be advised to use effective non-hormonal contraceptive methods. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 3. Ribociclib increases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is recommended. 4. Rifabutin decreases the levels of oral levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 5. Rifampin decreases the levels of oral levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Rifapentine decreases the levels of oral levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Ritonavir increases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 8. Rucaparib increases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. Adjust the dosage of CYP3A4 substrates if clinically indicated. 9. Siltuximab may restore CYP450 enzymatic activity by inhibiting IL-6, which is downregulated during infection and inflammation. Caution is advised when co-administering with CYP substrates that have a narrow therapeutic index. Monitor closely. 10. St. John’s Wort decreases the levels of oral levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 11. Stiripentol affects CYP3A4 metabolism as both an inhibitor and inducer. Monitor co-administered CYP3A4 substrates for increased or decreased effects. Dosage adjustments may be required. 12. Sugammadex sodium decreases the effects of oral levonorgestrel by competing for receptor binding. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. In vitro studies suggest sugammadex binds to progestogen, reducing its exposure. A bolus dose of sugammadex is equivalent to missing doses of hormonal contraceptives. Patients should use additional non-hormonal contraceptive methods (e.g., condoms and spermicides) for the next 7 days if oral contraceptives are taken on the same day as sugammadex or if the patient uses transdermal or implant hormonal contraceptives. 13. Tazemetostat decreases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Tecovirimat decreases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by weakly inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor sensitive CYP3A4 substrates for effectiveness if co-administered. 15. Teriflunomide increases the levels of oral levonorgestrel through an unknown mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 16. Tesamorelin decreases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by altering its metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. Consider alternative contraception. 17. Topiramate decreases the levels of oral levonorgestrel by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Tovorafenib decreases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by weakly inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration with hormonal contraceptives. If unavoidable, use an additional effective non-hormonal contraceptive method during co-administration and for 28 days after discontinuation. 19. Tucatinib increases the levels or effects of oral levonorgestrel by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration with CYP3A substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious or life-threatening toxicities. If unavoidable, reduce the CYP3A substrate dose according to product labeling. 20. Valoctocogene roxaparvovec and oral levonorgestrel both increase the risk of hepatotoxicity. Medications that may cause hepatotoxicity when combined with valoctocogene roxaparvovec should be closely monitored. Consider alternative medications in case of potential drug interactions. 21. Common side effects of levonorgestrel include headache (12%), acne (15%), ovarian cysts (13%), enlarged follicles (12%), amenorrhea (1–12%), abdominal pain (12%), uterine/vaginal bleeding alterations (52%), intermenstrual bleeding/spotting (23%), vulvovaginitis (20%), ectopic pregnancy (≤50%), depression (4%), migraine (2%), alopecia (1%), dysmenorrhea (9%), menorrhagia (6%), breast tenderness (3–9%), pelvic pain (6%), leukorrhea (5%), vaginal discharge (4%), pelvic infection (1%), angioedema, cervical perforation, failed insertion, sepsis, uterine bleeding, device breakage, and documented hypersensitivity. 22. Patients with a family history of breast cancer, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), or pulmonary embolism (PE), or those with current or past depression, endometriosis, diabetes mellitus (DM), hypertension (HTN), bone mineral density changes, renal/hepatic impairment, bone metabolic disease, or systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) should be monitored closely. Conditions exacerbated by fluid retention (e.g., migraine, asthma, epilepsy) should also be considered. 23. Discontinue levonorgestrel if jaundice, visual problems (e.g., contact lens intolerance), signs of venous thromboembolism (VTE), unusually severe migraines, significant blood pressure increases, or severe depression develop. Increased risk of thromboembolic complications after surgery warrants discontinuation 4 weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization. 24. Patients on warfarin or oral anticoagulants may require an increased anticoagulant dose. Some studies link oral contraceptive use with an increased risk of breast cancer, while others show no change. Risk depends on factors such as early menarche, late menopause, first childbirth after age 30, or nulliparity. 25. Oral contraceptive use may increase the risk of cervical cancer, but human papillomavirus (HPV) remains the primary risk factor. 26. Levonorgestrel is metabolized in the liver, with metabolites including tetrahydrolevonorgestrel, hydroxynorgestrel, and sulfate or glucuronide conjugates. Its half-life ranges from 11 to 45 hours, and it is excreted via urine (40–50%) and feces (32%). 27. Levonorgestrel is used to prevent pregnancy after birth control failure or unprotected sex. It may be less effective in women over 164 pounds (74 kg) or those who have used certain medications in the past month. This reduced effectiveness can result in pregnancy. 28. After taking levonorgestrel, menstrual timing and bleeding patterns may change. Notify your doctor if your period is more than 7 days late. 29. Side effects may include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tiredness, dizziness, changes in vaginal bleeding, breast tenderness, or headache. Serious allergic reactions are rare. Contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. 30. Levonorgestrel should not be used during pregnancy. It passes into breast milk but is unlikely to harm a nursing infant.
